title: Power From the Moon's Pull
question: How can the rise and fall of the tides be turned into electricity?
hook: Wind, solar, wave and fossil fuel energy all trace back to the Sun, but the tides draw on the orbits of the Earth and Moon.
idea: Tidal power captures energy from the regular, Moon-driven rise and fall of the sea, either with turbines in moving currents or with dams that hold back high water.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of a tidal barrage's power cycle in order.
items: The tide comes in and the sea rises
Water fills the basin behind the dam
The tide starts to go out
Stored water rushes through turbines to make power
beats.explain: A barrage catches the incoming tide in a basin, then releases the water through turbines as the tide recedes.

beats.prompt: Sort each energy source by whether its energy comes from the Sun.
groups: Does not come from the Sun
items: Does not come from the Sun
Does not come from the Sun
Does not come from the Sun
beats.explain: Wind, wave and fossil fuel energy originate from the Sun, while tidal power draws on the Earth–Moon orbits, geothermal on Earth's internal heat and nuclear on fissionable minerals.

beats.prompt: As tides flow, water is pumped through narrow coastal passages and loses energy to friction at the seabed, draining the Earth–Moon system. Over hundreds of millions of years, what happens to the length of a day?

choices.label: Days get shorter
choices.feedback: Losing energy slows Earth's spin rather than speeding it up.

choices.label: Days stay at 24 hours
choices.feedback: 620 million years ago a day lasted only 21.9 hours.

beats.explain: The energy loss has slowed Earth's rotation, so the day grew from 21.9 to 24 hours over the last 620 million years.

beats.prompt: Match each tidal project or design to what it is known for.
pairs: Ground grain as the tide went out
beats.explain: Tide mills date back to at least the Middle Ages, while power stations and lagoon walls are newer ways to tap the same tides.
